On June 20, 2023, the assistant explained Starling forces: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the interstitial space, while plasma oncotic pressure—maintained by proteins such as albumin—pulls fluid into capillaries. An imbalance can cause edema; heart failure can raise capillary hydrostatic pressure, and liver disease can lower oncotic pressure by reducing albumin production.

On June 20, 2023, the assistant defined thrombosis as formation of a blood clot (thrombus) within a blood vessel that may obstruct blood flow. Inappropriate clotting can follow disrupted blood flow or vessel-lining damage and cause ischemia or infarction. Common sites include deep veins of the legs and coronary arteries. Risk factors listed included advanced age, obesity, smoking, cancer, autoimmune disorders, and genetic clotting disorders. Treatments may include anticoagulants, thrombectomy, or angioplasty.

On June 20, 2023, the assistant classified thrombosis by location as arterial, venous, cardiac, or microvascular. Examples and consequences described included coronary, cerebral, and peripheral arterial thrombosis; leg DVT with possible pulmonary embolism; cardiac thrombi associated with atrial fibrillation, dilated cardiomyopathy, or artificial heart valves; and microvascular thrombosis associated with thrombotic microangiopathy, DIC, or sickle cell disease.

On June 20, 2023, the assistant described thrombus morphology: color can range from red or dark red in fresh RBC-rich thrombi to paler in older or organized thrombi; consistency can be firm or friable; shape may be cylindrical, conical, or branching; thrombi may adhere to the vessel wall or float in the lumen. With time, thrombi may organize into fibrous scar with fibroblasts and blood vessels, or undergo recanalization, forming channels that can restore some blood flow.

On June 20, 2023, the assistant described venous thrombi as clots of platelets, fibrin, red blood cells, and leukocytes, commonly forming in deep leg or pelvic veins. DVT may cause limb swelling, pain, warmth, and redness, or be asymptomatic until pulmonary embolism causes shortness of breath and chest pain. Virchow’s triad comprises blood-flow stasis (for example, immobility, varicose veins, or surgery), endothelial injury (for example, trauma, infection, or toxins), and hypercoagulability (for example, cancer, pregnancy, hormonal therapy, or genetic disorders such as factor V Leiden mutation or antithrombin III deficiency). Acute venous thrombi are relatively soft and friable, mainly composed of RBCs and fibrin; older thrombi become organized and fibrotic, with neovascularization. The assistant gave an incidence estimate of up to 1 per 1,000 person-years.

On 23 August 2018, the Builder issued invoice 104 for $156,113.54. Mrs Cappello replied that day that the work was close to finalisation but incomplete, said she had told her husband not to pay anything until all work was completed, and listed work she said remained incomplete. The plaintiffs later paid $75,000 toward invoice 104; the date of payment was unclear, and they did not pay the $81,113.54 balance.

On 10 October 2018, the Builder’s solicitors sent the plaintiffs a notice titled “Notice of Dispute and Notice of Suspension of Works” concerning non-payment of invoice 104 and requesting a meeting to resolve the dispute. After a meeting could not be arranged, the solicitors sent a “Notice of Breach of Contract” by registered post on 18 October 2018. It alleged breach of clause 15.6 for failure to pay the $81,113.54 balance and gave ten working days to remedy the breach under clause 24, failing which the Builder might end the Contract. The plaintiffs did not pay, and on 20 November 2018 the solicitors sent a registered “Notice of Termination of Contract.” The court held that the termination notice was effective; the plaintiffs made no submission explaining why it was ineffective.

The Builder relied on a report by expert quantity surveyor Michael Sturgess. After inspecting the work and invoices, Sturgess assessed a reasonable value for the Builder’s work at $555,942.66, exceeding the $544,743.92 paid to or claimed by the Builder. He identified the work from supplied documents and his own measurements, used Rawlinsons Australian Construction Handbook 2018 (36th edition) and his own knowledge to cost it, and applied labour rates of $90 per hour for plumbing and electrical trades and $70 per hour for other trades.

The plaintiffs argued that Michael Sturgess’s report was based on quantum meruit, while the Builder’s claim was contractual, and relied on Mann v Paterson Constructions Pty Ltd (2019) 373 ALR 1; [2019] HCA 32 at [19]. The court explained that the report created a false issue: under the Contract the Builder could claim periodic payments upon presenting invoices, and the Builder did not have to prove that its invoiced charges were reasonable. The plaintiffs could instead defend invoice 104 by showing, for example, that the claimed work was outside the Contract, had not been done, or was not calculated according to the Contract. Without such a defence, the plaintiffs had to pay the invoice balance.
entities: Mann v Paterson Constructions Pty Ltd
records.topic: Contractual payment claims versus quantum meruit

records.text: The court held that the Builder’s claim for work performed before termination but not yet invoiced was properly a claim for damages arising from termination. The Builder should ordinarily have proved what additional work it performed after the work covered by invoice 104 and what it could have charged for that work under the Contract. Instead, it relied on an assessment of the reasonable value of all work on a quantum meruit basis. The evidence did not establish precisely what post-invoice-104 work was done or the contractual amount chargeable, and a reasonable-value assessment of all work could not fill that evidentiary gap. The court therefore concluded that this evidence did not prove the Builder’s claim for the unbilled work.
records.topic: Unbilled work and damages after termination

records.text: Subject to any offsetting claim, the Builder was entitled to recover $81,113.54, the unpaid balance of invoice 104. The excerpt does not establish that the Builder recovered its separate claim for unbilled work.
